svg.title: Turbulence: three causes and four intensities
svg.desc: Three causes: convective or thermal turbulence from heated ground, worst on warm afternoons under cumulus; mechanical turbulence from wind over buildings, trees and hills near the ground; and wind shear or clear air turbulence from sharp changes of wind speed or direction near fronts, inversions and the jet stream. Intensity per the AIM: light, moderate, severe and extreme. In moderate or worse turbulence slow to maneuvering speed.
svg.text: Turbulence: three causes and four intensities
Turbulence comes from three common causes. Know the cause to know where to expect it.
Slow down to maneuvering speed (VA) when you meet moderate or worse turbulence.
Convective (thermal)
Heated ground sends up thermals
and the cooler air sinks between them.
Worst on warm afternoons under
cumulus. Fly early, or above the tops.
Mechanical (low level)
Wind flowing over buildings, trees and
hills breaks into eddies. It is gusty near
the ground, worst in strong winds, and
makes takeoffs and landings rough.
Wind shear and clear air
A sharp change in wind speed or
direction over a short distance: near
fronts, inversions and the jet stream.
Clear air turbulence gives no cloud warning.
fast
slower, other way
Turbulence intensity (AIM pilot reports)
Light
Slight, erratic changes in altitude or attitude. Occupants may feel a
slight strain against belts.
Moderate
Changes in altitude or attitude, airspeed varies a little, aircraft stays
in positive control. Definite strain on belts.
Severe
Large, abrupt changes; airspeed varies greatly; control may be briefly
lost. Occupants are forced into belts.
Extreme
Violently tossed about, practically impossible to control. May cause
structural damage.
